header.name: Political Anthropology: State and Subject
header.description: To do well in this course requires a lot of reading and intellectual application. This is a hard 2xx level class. This course is an examination of politics as an activity constitutive of humanness. The course introduces students to foundational problems in political anthropology. Order, sovereignty and contestation, government, State and subject are key categories we will examine. Our first question: can there be order in the absence of a government, state, leader, sovereign? We then examine order in the context of empire and kingship, with case studies from Asia and Europe. Next, we trace the emergence of 'government' as a (modern) project of order in the political history of Europe. We look at how systems of political order are transformed during the period of Colonial rule/governance. We will then see the centrality of bureaucracy to modern governance. The second half of the course opens with inquiries into the central political forms of modern history is the 'nation' and the constitution. If constitution is one side, insurrection is its other side and we examine how both are constitutive of 'democracy'. Taking violence as an analytical object, we study the state (and its apparatuses of subjection) at the margins, treading at the limits of legality. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the political, that is, politics as the distinction between friend and enemy. Another way to look at this course: a survey of forms of power, and the forms of subjection produced in persons subject to power. By the end of the course, students will be able to come up with a nuanced, reasoned analyses of complex problems of politics, drawing on conceptual models developed in this class.
